clinicalPearls: Minimal change disease accounts for the large majority of idiopathic nephrotic syndrome in children, most commonly presenting between about 1 and 6 years of age.
The defining features are heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, and hyperlipidaemia.
Oedema is typically dependent and periorbital and can progress to generalised swelling with ascites and pleural effusions.
Most children are steroid-responsive, and a favourable response to corticosteroids is both diagnostic and therapeutic in the typical age group.

Renal biopsy is generally reserved for atypical features such as age under 1 or over 10 years, persistent hypertension, gross haematuria, low complement, impaired renal function, or steroid resistance.
Children are at increased risk of infection, particularly spontaneous bacterial peritonitis from encapsulated organisms, because of urinary immunoglobulin losses.
A hypercoagulable state develops from urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins, increasing the risk of venous and arterial thrombosis.
Relapses are common, and some children become frequent relapsers or steroid-dependent, requiring steroid-sparing agents.
reference.pathophysiology: A poorly understood immune dysregulation, involving circulating permeability factors and T-cell mediated signalling, injures the glomerular podocytes. On light microscopy the glomeruli appear normal, but electron microscopy reveals diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes. Loss of the size- and charge-selective filtration barrier permits massive albumin leakage into the urine, producing hypoalbuminaemia, reduced oncotic pressure, oedema, and compensatory hepatic lipoprotein synthesis causing hyperlipidaemia.
additionalInvestigations: Urinalysis and quantification of proteinuria (protein:creatinine ratio or 24-hour protein)
Serum albumin, lipid profile, and renal function
Autoimmune serology when secondary causes are suspected
Assessment for infection and, in selected cases, screening for thrombosis
Renal biopsy in atypical presentations or steroid resistance
redFlags: Signs of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (fever, abdominal pain, tenderness)
Features of venous or arterial thrombosis, including limb swelling, respiratory compromise, or neurological signs
Severe respiratory distress from large pleural effusions or ascites
Steroid resistance or deteriorating renal function suggesting a more aggressive lesion
reference.prognosis: Children with steroid-sensitive minimal change disease generally have an excellent long-term renal prognosis, though many experience relapses over several years before remitting; steroid-resistant disease, often reflecting focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, carries a higher risk of progression to chronic kidney disease.
pitfalls: Missing spontaneous bacterial peritonitis because ascitic signs can be subtle in an oedematous child
Overlooking thrombosis risk during periods of heavy proteinuria and diuresis
Assuming all childhood nephrotic syndrome is minimal change and delaying biopsy in atypical cases
Over-diuresing and precipitating hypovolaemia in a child with low intravascular volume
management: Induce remission with oral corticosteroids (prednisolone), which are both diagnostic and therapeutic in the typical age group
For frequent relapses or steroid dependence, add steroid-sparing agents such as levamisole, calcineurin inhibitors (ciclosporin or tacrolimus), mycophenolate mofetil, cyclophosphamide or rituximab
Manage oedema with dietary sodium restriction and diuretics, reserving intravenous albumin for severe symptomatic oedema
Treat infections promptly, remaining alert to spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, and ensure pneumococcal and other vaccination
Consider thromboprophylaxis in severe nephrotic states given the hypercoagulable risk
Monitor for relapse with home urine dipstick testing, and track growth and corticosteroid side effects
Refer for renal biopsy and specialist input in atypical presentations or steroid-resistant disease, which may reflect focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
